item.title: Fell flat at the end
item.content:encoded: Past the little issues others have pointed out about terminology, I believe the greatest problem lies in the termination of the subject. It feels extremely out of character for the foundation, opting to kill rather than examine and question. The foundation wants to learn as much as possible, and by destroying all sources of information, they would lose the ability to do so. It’s a shame, since the SCP is intriguing otherwise, but it seems like the writer just got bored and wanted to end it there. And seeing as it’s s1, where most people spend most of their time reading (let’s just be realistic), it sets a bad precedent.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
• Carbide lamp
  • Bulb
  • Battery compartment

(oh, huh… inline tagging using greater-than signs apparently doesn't work here and just makes everything on the line invisible… had to edit it to use bullets instead)

Six years since Agent Angus Smith first pointed out this howler of a mistake, and it's still there. Is there no way to alter the article to take account of the fact that "carbide" lamps aren't a brand name but instead indicate something that produces and burns acetylene, and has no electrical components whatsoever? It's not even like it refers to the aesthetic style of the thing (although the picture is clearly either such a gas-lamp, or an electric one carefully styled to look just like one for, er, no good reason whatsoever other than nostalgia, with a carefully hidden bulb and a somewhat snug battery compartment externally decorated to look like the gas production/storage chamber), it's literally just a designation of how it works, the same as "electric lantern" or "oil lamp" would be. You put calcium carbide crystals and water into it to make gas…

Threw me right off at the start of the article and, well, can't really comment on the rest of it because I wasn't able to shake the disconnect.

Change need only be slight, e.g. describing it as an electric lantern styled after a turn-of-the-20th-century acetylene fuelled "carbide" lamp, or that although it otherwise resembles such a lamp in form and function (eg how you turn it on involving turning a tap and pressing a spark-lighter button), appears to show a dancing flame when looked into and has a light spectrum equivalent to that of other carbide lamps but was found to contain an ordinary low-voltage torch bulb and a set of seemingly wrongly connected D-cells when disassembled (thus furthering its anomalous nature)… or just biting the bullet, finding a picture of an actual brass era electric lantern, and changing "carbide" to (whatever that model's brand name was, plus?) "electric".

(is it also worth mentioning that old electric lanterns tended to use cuboid 6-volt batteries with four internal cells sealed inside them, and tubular flashlights using cylindrical "radio" cells were a somewhat later invention from somewhere in the bakelite age?)

item.content:encoded:
I like this one. There are minor technical problems. Carbide lamps don't use bulbs, circuits, or batteries. According to Wikipedia,

Carbide lamps, or acetylene gas lamps, are simple lamps that produce and burn acetylene (C2H2) which is created by the reaction of calcium carbide (CaC2) with water.

Simply stating that the lamp has been modified into an electrical light would fix this. Describing it as made in the style of an old carbide lamp would also work.

Bronze and brass are two distinctly different alloys. The Late 19th and Early 20th century used brass almost exclusively over bronze. A lamp made of bronze is certainly possible, especially if homemade.
